title: The Perception by University Students of the Use of ChatGPT in Education
venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ perceptions of ChatGPT in education, focusing on perceived benefits, barriers, and possible ways to use the tool more effectively. The study was motivated by the rapid rise of generative AI in education and a lack of empirical evidence about how students actually experience ChatGPT in academic work.

The authors used a mixed-methods design with an online questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The sample consisted of 200 Vietnamese university students who had previously used ChatGPT for academic purposes; 30 of these students were interviewed. The survey used 5-point Likert items and the data were analyzed with descriptive statistics and one-sample t-tests, while interview responses were coded into themes.

Results indicated generally positive perceptions of ChatGPT. Students strongly agreed that it is easy to use, can function as a search engine, can work across languages, and is useful for study. Reported benefits included saving time, accessing information across diverse fields, improving writing through idea generation and feedback, and providing personalized tutoring/adaptive learning. Reported barriers centered on reliability and academic accuracy, such as inability to verify source quality, cite correctly, handle idioms well, and deal with difficult mathematical formulas. Students suggested verifying responses against reliable sources, using ChatGPT as a consultant rather than copying answers, providing clear guidelines, and promoting academic integrity. The study did not test learning outcomes or compare ChatGPT with a control group; it mainly documents perceptions and concerns among students.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative language model / conversational chatbot for natural-language interaction, text generation, and instructional assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed university students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT for learning, including perceived benefits, barriers, and suggested solutions; also interviewed a subset of students about their experiences.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported generally favorable perceptions of ChatGPT for learning (general mean=3.61/5; use of ChatGPT mean=3.62). The one-sample t-test showed the mean was significantly above the neutral point of 3 (t=31.868, df=199, p=0.000).
findings.measure: Overall perception/use of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

findings.finding_summary: Students perceived several benefits of ChatGPT in learning, with an overall benefits mean of 3.58/5. Highest-rated benefits were saving time (mean=3.74) and providing information in diverse fields (mean=3.66). The one-sample t-test indicated the benefits score was significantly above neutral (t=18.051, df=199, p=0.000).
findings.measure: Perceived benefits of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

findings.finding_summary: Students also reported barriers, with an overall barriers mean of 3.64/5. Top concerns were inability to examine source quality/reliability (mean=3.73), inability to replace words and use idioms wisely (mean=3.72), and inability to handle difficult mathematical formulas (mean=3.72). The barriers score was significantly above neutral (t=27.331, df=199, p=0.000), indicating substantial concern as well as perceived usefulness.
findings.measure: Perceived barriers/limitations of ChatGPT on a 5-point Likert scale

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods perception study with survey and interviews, not a controlled intervention study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about perceived benefits and barriers, but it does not test causal effects of ChatGPT coaching or feedback.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions of ChatGPT and specific perceived affordances such as time-saving and personalized tutoring/feedback, but there are no outcome effect sizes on learning. The practical impact is therefore suggestive but unquantified.
